Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The Czech Republic's practice of surgically castrating convicted sex offenders is "invasive, irreversible and mutilating" and should stop immediately, the Council of Europe's Anti-Torture Committee said in a report made public Thursday. The central European country castrated at least 94 prisoners in the 10 years up to April 2008, when investigators from the Council of Europe, a human-rights forum, visited the Czech Republic. The Council of Europe condemned the practice as "degrading." The procedure is being performed even on first-time, non-violent offenders, such as exhibitionists, its investigation revealed. Prisoners have to request castration under Czech law, but many fear they will be jailed for life if they do not, the investigation found. "In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention," the report said. "Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention." And it warned that some "significantly" mentally retarded people had been castrated. "In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated," the report said. "In all of these instances, the court-appointed guardian had signed the consent form; in two cases, the guardians were mayors." The investigators found only two convicts who had spontaneously volunteered for castration, while others they interviewed said mental health staff specializing in sexuality had recommended it. "The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient's admission to hospital," the report said. "Some of the sexologists interviewed by the delegation themselves affirmed that for certain patients there was no alternative treatment to surgical castration." The Czech Republic defends the practice as voluntary, saying castration aims permanently to reduce testosterone levels in order to diminish the offender's sexual urges. The process, officially called "therapeutic testicular pulpectomies ... are performed upon a written request of an adult man," the Czech government responded. It said the operation had to be approved by a committee of experts. "Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive," the Czech government said, saying the Council of Europe had not proven its case sufficiently for the country to abandon castration. It argues the procedure is effective in reducing repeat offenses. But the Council of Europe questioned the statistics on repeat offenses and said even if they were correct, castration was not an appropriate way to reduce recidivism. "The committee's delegation came across three cases in which sex offenders had committed serious sex-related crimes, including serial rape and attempted murder, after they had been surgically castrated," the human-rights group said. "Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders," the report said. It said candidates for castration often received information about the procedure which was too technical to understand -- or no information at all. "Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed," the report warned. It condemned the practice as "an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis," also warning of possible depression and changes in appearance. It said it was impossible to determine how many people had been castrated in keeping with a 1966 law. The Council of Europe delegation visited the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008. It issued its report and the Czech response on July 23, 2008. It made them public on Thursday at the request of the Czech government, it said.

The Central European country castrated at least 94 prisoners in the decade leading up to April 2008, when investigators from the Council of Europe, a human-rights forum, visited the Czech Republic. The Council of Europe condemned the practice as “degrading.”

Its investigation found that the procedure has been performed even on first-time, non-violent offenders, including exhibitionists. Under Czech law, prisoners must request castration, but investigators found that many feared they would otherwise be detained for life.

“In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention,” the report said. “Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention.”

The report also warned that some people with “significant” mental disabilities had been castrated. “In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated,” it said. “In all of these instances, the court-appointed guardian had signed the consent form; in two cases, the guardians were mayors.”

Investigators found only two convicts who had volunteered for castration spontaneously. Others interviewed said mental health professionals specializing in sexuality had recommended the procedure.

“The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient’s admission to hospital,” the report said. “Some of the sexologists interviewed by the delegation themselves affirmed that for certain patients there was no alternative treatment to surgical castration.”

The Czech Republic has defended the practice as voluntary, saying castration is intended to permanently reduce testosterone levels in order to diminish offenders’ sexual urges. The procedure, officially described as “therapeutic testicular pulpectomies,” is “performed upon a written request of an adult man,” the Czech government said in its response.

The government said the operation must be approved by a committee of experts. “Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive,” it said, adding that the Council of Europe had not sufficiently proven its case for the Czech Republic to abandon the practice.

The Czech government also argued that the procedure is effective in reducing repeat offenses. However, the Council of Europe questioned the statistics on recidivism and said that, even if the figures were accurate, castration was not an appropriate means of reducing reoffending.

“The committee’s delegation came across three cases in which sex offenders had committed serious sex-related crimes, including serial rape and attempted murder, after they had been surgically castrated,” the human-rights group said.

“Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders,” the report stated.

The report also said that candidates for castration often received information about the procedure that was too technical to understand—or, in some cases, received no information at all.

“Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed,” the report warned.

It condemned the practice as “an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis,” while also warning of possible depression and changes in appearance.

The report said it was impossible to determine how many people had been castrated under a 1966 law. The Council of Europe delegation visited the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008. (CNN) — The Council of Europe’s Anti-Torture Committee has called on the Czech Republic to end without delay its policy of surgically castrating convicted sex offenders, describing the procedure as “invasive, irreversible and mutilating.” Its report, released publicly on Thursday, also characterized the practice as “degrading.”

According to the Council of Europe, a human-rights organization, Czech authorities castrated at least 94 inmates during the decade leading up to April 2008, when its investigators visited the country. The inquiry found that the operation had been carried out not only on violent repeat offenders, but also on people convicted for the first time and for non-violent sexual offenses, including exhibitionism.

Under Czech law, prisoners must formally ask to undergo castration. However, the investigation concluded that many did so because they feared they would otherwise remain imprisoned for life. “In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention,” the report stated. “Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention.”

The committee also raised concern that some offenders with significant mental disabilities had undergone the operation. “In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated,” the report said. “In all of these instances, the court-appointed guardian had signed the consent form; in two cases, the guardians were mayors.”

Investigators said they found only two prisoners who had volunteered for castration without prompting. Other inmates interviewed said the idea had been proposed by mental-health professionals specializing in sexual behavior. “The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient’s admission to hospital,” the report said. It added that some sexologists interviewed by the delegation maintained that, for certain patients, no treatment other than surgical castration was available.

The Czech government has defended the procedure as voluntary. It says the purpose is to permanently lower testosterone levels and thereby reduce offenders’ sexual drives. In its official response, the government said the operation, formally known as “therapeutic testicular pulpectomies,” is carried out only after “a written request of an adult man.”

Authorities also said the operation requires approval from a committee of specialists. “Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive,” the Czech government said. It argued that the Council of Europe had not made a strong enough case to justify ending the practice, and said castration helps prevent reoffending.

The Council of Europe disputed the Czech figures on repeat offenses and said that, even if the statistics were accurate, surgical castration would still be an unacceptable method of reducing recidivism. The group said its delegation encountered three cases in which sex offenders committed serious sexual crimes after being surgically castrated, including serial rape and attempted murder.

“Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders,” the report said. It also found that men being considered for the operation were often given explanations that were too technical to understand, or in some cases received no information at all. “Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed,” the committee warned.

The report criticized the procedure as “an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis.” It also noted possible consequences including depression and changes in physical appearance.

The committee said it could not determine the total number of people castrated under a Czech law dating back to 1966. The Council of Europe delegation visited the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008. The report and the Czech government’s response were issued on July 23, 2008, and were made public on Thursday at the request of the Czech authorities.

The Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment examined the Czech Republic’s use of surgical castration as a measure applied to certain convicted sex offenders. Its inquiry looked at individual cases, the legal and medical procedures surrounding the practice, the way consent was obtained, and the broader treatment recommendations made by doctors and authorities. The Committee was particularly concerned that surgical castration was being presented as part of a therapeutic response to sexual offending, even though it is a drastic medical intervention with permanent physical and psychological consequences.

The Committee found that the practice was highly invasive and irreversible. It noted that surgical castration fundamentally alters a person’s body and bodily integrity, and that its effects cannot be compared to less intrusive forms of treatment, such as psychotherapy or reversible medication. Because of the seriousness of the procedure, the Committee scrutinized whether those subjected to it had truly given free and informed consent.

Its findings raised serious doubts about the voluntariness of that consent. In several cases, offenders were offered castration in circumstances where refusal could affect their prospects of release, detention conditions, or future treatment decisions. The Committee considered that such pressure could make consent coercive rather than genuinely voluntary. It also observed that some individuals who underwent or were considered for the procedure were in vulnerable positions, including persons with mental incapacity or limited ability to understand the consequences of the operation.

The Committee was especially troubled by the fact that surgical castration was not limited to the most extreme cases. It found that the measure had been applied or recommended even for first-time offenders, non-violent offenders, and people whose offences did not demonstrate the level of danger that might be used to justify severe preventive measures. This suggested that the practice was being used too broadly and without sufficient safeguards.

In the Committee’s view, surgical castration of detained or convicted persons amounted to degrading treatment. It emphasized that punishment or public protection cannot justify medical procedures that violate human dignity, bodily integrity, and fundamental rights. The permanent and mutilating nature of the intervention, combined with the coercive context in which decisions were often made, made the practice incompatible with modern human-rights standards.

The Committee therefore urged the Czech authorities to bring the practice to an immediate end. It recommended that surgical castration no longer be used as a treatment or risk-management measure for sex offenders and that the authorities instead rely on humane, evidence-based, and reversible forms of therapy and supervision. The Committee’s conclusion was clear: the surgical castration of sex offenders, particularly in coercive or insufficiently safeguarded circumstances, constitutes a serious human-rights violation and should be abolished.

**Council of Europe panel condemns Czech surgical castration of sex offenders**

*Prague, Czech Republic (CNN) —* The Council of Europe’s anti-torture watchdog has sharply criticized the Czech Republic for allowing the surgical castration of convicted sex offenders, calling the practice “degrading” and urging authorities to end it immediately.

In a report on the Czech Republic, the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment — known as the CPT — said surgical castration is an irreversible and “mutilating” intervention that cannot be justified as a treatment for people in state custody.

The committee said it had examined cases involving sex offenders held in psychiatric facilities and detention settings, where consent to the procedure could not be considered fully free because some patients faced the prospect of long-term or indefinite confinement.

“The CPT has fundamental objections to the use of surgical castration as a means of treatment of sex offenders,” the report said, calling on Czech authorities to abolish the practice.

According to the report, Czech officials acknowledged that surgical castration had been carried out on a number of offenders over the years, including men convicted of serious sexual crimes. The procedure involves removal of the testes, drastically reducing testosterone production and sexual drive.

The CPT said it was particularly concerned that some offenders may have agreed to castration under pressure, believing it would improve their chances of release from psychiatric treatment or detention. The committee also noted that less invasive alternatives exist, including psychotherapy and hormone-based treatment, sometimes referred to as “chemical castration,” which is reversible.

Czech authorities defended the practice, saying it is performed only in exceptional cases, with the consent of the offender and after medical and legal review. The government argued that surgical castration can be an effective treatment for certain high-risk sex offenders and can help protect the public from reoffending.

Officials also said the procedure is not imposed as a punishment and is subject to approval by expert bodies. They maintained that offenders are informed of the consequences and that the operation may, in some cases, offer an alternative to prolonged institutional confinement.

But the CPT rejected that reasoning, saying the circumstances surrounding detention and possible release cast doubt on whether consent can truly be voluntary.

The committee urged the Czech Republic to stop surgical castration of detained sex offenders and to rely instead on treatment methods that respect human dignity and bodily integrity.

The Council of Europe, based in Strasbourg, France, is a human rights organization separate from the European Union. Its anti-torture committee conducts visits to prisons, psychiatric hospitals and other places of detention across member states and issues reports with recommendations to governments.

**Council of Europe faults Czech surgical castration of sex offenders, citing consent and rights concerns**

**PRAGUE/STRASBOURG —** A Council of Europe monitoring body has sharply criticized the Czech Republic for allowing the surgical castration of convicted sex offenders, warning that the practice raises serious human-rights concerns and that the “consent” of detainees may not be genuinely free when it is offered as a route out of prolonged confinement.

In a report following visits to Czech detention and psychiatric facilities, the Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) said the Czech authorities had continued to permit the irreversible removal of testicular tissue from some sex offenders, a procedure the committee described as mutilating and unacceptable in the modern treatment of offenders.

The CPT said it was particularly concerned that surgical castration was being used in a criminal-justice and psychiatric context, where men subject to court-ordered treatment could face extended or indeterminate detention. In such circumstances, the committee said, a patient’s agreement to the operation may be influenced by the prospect of release or transfer to less restrictive conditions, calling into question whether consent is truly voluntary.

The investigation focused on offenders held under protective treatment orders, including men considered to pose a continuing risk of sexual violence. The CPT said surgical castration had been presented in some cases as a therapeutic measure aimed at reducing libido and the risk of reoffending. But it emphasized that the operation is irreversible and that less invasive alternatives exist, including psychotherapy, structured risk management and anti-androgen medication, often referred to as “chemical castration,” which is reversible when treatment stops.

Human-rights advocates have long argued that surgical castration of offenders — even where formally authorized by law and accompanied by signed consent — is inherently coercive if the alternative is continued confinement. The CPT echoed that concern, saying the imbalance of power between detained patients and the state, combined with the desire to regain liberty, can place heavy pressure on offenders to accept a procedure they might otherwise refuse.

The committee called on the Czech Republic to end the use of surgical castration in the treatment of sex offenders and to bring its practices into line with European human-rights standards. It said any medical intervention must be based on free and informed consent, independent medical assessment and respect for human dignity.

Czech officials rejected suggestions that the procedure amounted to abuse, saying surgical castration was rare, lawful and performed only after multiple safeguards. Authorities said candidates must request the operation themselves, receive medical information about its consequences, and obtain approval from an expert commission. They also argued that the measure had been used only in serious cases involving offenders with severe sexual disorders and a high risk of reoffending.

Officials maintained that the Czech system was designed to protect the public while offering treatment to offenders who might otherwise remain in secure psychiatric care. They said the operation was not imposed as a punishment and was not carried out without consent.

The CPT, however, said the formal existence of consent forms and review panels did not resolve the central problem. In its view, a detained offender’s decision is compromised if refusal may result in continued institutionalization. The committee also questioned whether surgical castration can ever be justified as a medical treatment in such circumstances, given its irreversible nature and the availability of other options.

The dispute places the Czech Republic at odds with a key Council of Europe watchdog responsible for monitoring treatment of detainees and preventing torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. While the CPT’s findings are not court judgments, its reports carry significant weight among European governments and human-rights bodies.

The issue has drawn attention beyond the Czech Republic because it sits at the intersection of public safety, medical ethics and the rights of people deprived of liberty. Supporters of strict measures for repeat sex offenders argue that governments have a duty to prevent further attacks. Critics respond that punishment and preventive detention cannot justify permanent bodily alteration under pressure from the state.

The Council of Europe urged Prague to abandon surgical castration and rely instead on treatment methods compatible with human-rights norms. Czech authorities said they would continue to review their policies but defended the existing safeguards and stressed that any such procedure remained exceptional.

Human rights groups and European oversight bodies have argued that offenders may have been **pressured into consenting** to the procedure. The controversy intensified after reports by the **Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture**, which criticized the practice and urged Czech authorities to end it. The committee said surgical castration can amount to degrading treatment when performed under coercive circumstances and warned that irreversible procedures should not be used as a condition for release or improved treatment status.

The government has argued that testicular pulpectomy significantly lowers testosterone levels and can reduce the likelihood that high-risk sexual offenders will commit further crimes. But opponents counter that public-safety goals do not justify irreversible surgery if offenders feel they have no real alternative. They have called for reliance on less invasive treatments, such as psychotherapy, hormonal medication and supervised reintegration programs.

The dispute highlights a broader tension in criminal justice and medical ethics: how to balance the protection of the public with the rights, dignity and bodily autonomy of offenders undergoing treatment.

# Council of Europe Publishes Report Criticizing Czech Surgical Castration Practices for Sex Offenders

**STRASBOURG —** The Council of Europe has made public a sharply critical report on the Czech Republic’s use of surgical castration in the treatment of sex offenders, raising concerns over the procedure’s use on mentally incapacitated offenders, the reliability of “informed consent” in custodial settings, and the serious medical and ethical risks associated with an irreversible operation.

The report, issued by the Council of Europe’s **Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment** — widely known as the **CPT** — follows a delegation visit to the Czech Republic during which inspectors examined the treatment of detained persons, including offenders undergoing psychiatric or sexological treatment.

The CPT said Czech authorities had continued to permit surgical castration — the removal or disabling of the testes — in certain cases involving sex offenders, despite the committee’s longstanding view that the practice is “invasive, irreversible and mutilating” and should not be used as a treatment measure in detention or forensic psychiatric contexts.

## Concerns Over Mentally Incapacitated Offenders

One of the report’s most serious findings concerns the possibility that surgical castration has been carried out on offenders whose mental condition called into question their ability to understand or freely agree to the operation.

The CPT highlighted cases involving individuals with significant mental impairment or psychiatric disorders who were subject to protective treatment. In such circumstances, the committee said, genuine consent is especially difficult to establish.

The report raises concerns that some offenders may not have had the full mental capacity to weigh the permanent consequences of castration, including its physical, psychological and sexual effects. Where a detained person is mentally incapacitated, the CPT suggested, reliance on formal consent — or consent mediated through guardians, medical boards or court-related procedures — may be insufficient to protect the person’s rights.

The committee stressed that the issue is not merely whether a form was signed or whether domestic procedures were followed, but whether the person concerned was truly able to make a free, informed and competent decision.

## Informed Consent Questioned in Detention Settings

The CPT also questioned whether consent to surgical castration can be considered genuinely voluntary when given by offenders detained in prisons, psychiatric hospitals or secure treatment facilities.

In the Czech system examined by the delegation, offenders could face long-term confinement under protective treatment measures. The CPT warned that, in such a setting, detainees may perceive castration as a route to release, better treatment conditions or a more favorable assessment by courts and medical authorities.

That dynamic, the committee said, can create powerful pressure on offenders to accept the operation — even if formally presented as voluntary.

Human-rights bodies have long argued that consent obtained in custodial environments requires heightened scrutiny, particularly when the proposed intervention is irreversible and affects bodily integrity. The CPT said Czech safeguards did not adequately dispel concerns that some offenders may have consented under implicit coercion.

The committee also questioned whether patients were always fully informed about alternative treatments, the limits of surgical castration in preventing reoffending, and the long-term consequences of the operation.

## Medical Risks and Irreversible Consequences

The report underlines that surgical castration carries serious and permanent medical implications.

Among the risks and consequences identified in discussions of the practice are:

- irreversible loss of testicular function;
- infertility;
- major hormonal changes;
- reduced or eliminated sexual drive, though not necessarily elimination of all sexual capacity or risk;
- osteoporosis and other bone-density problems;
- metabolic and cardiovascular complications;
- hot flashes, fatigue and weight changes;
- depression or other psychological effects;
- surgical risks such as bleeding, infection and complications from anesthesia.

The CPT emphasized that surgical castration is not a guaranteed method of preventing sexual reoffending. While testosterone reduction can diminish libido, the committee noted that sexual violence and offending behavior are complex phenomena that cannot be addressed solely through irreversible surgery.

The committee pointed to less invasive alternatives, including psychotherapy, behavioral treatment, psychiatric care and reversible anti-androgen medication, often described as “chemical castration,” though that too requires strict safeguards, monitoring and consent.

## CPT Calls for an End to the Practice

The Council of Europe committee urged Czech authorities to stop using surgical castration as a treatment option for detained sex offenders.

The CPT’s position is that the practice is incompatible with modern standards for the treatment of persons deprived of liberty, particularly because of its irreversible character and the risk that consent may be compromised.

The committee has previously criticized the Czech Republic over the same issue, making this report part of a longer-running dispute between European human-rights monitors and Czech medical and legal authorities.

Czech officials have historically defended the procedure as rare, regulated and performed only with consent and approval by medical specialists. Supporters within the Czech forensic treatment system have argued that, in selected cases, surgical castration may reduce reoffending risk and allow certain offenders to leave secure treatment.

But the CPT rejected those arguments, saying the procedure’s human-rights implications outweigh claimed benefits, especially where vulnerable or mentally impaired detainees are involved.

## Timeline of the Delegation’s Visit

According to the report, the CPT delegation carried out its visit to the Czech Republic as part of its monitoring mandate under the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture.

The delegation’s work followed the standard CPT process:

1. **On-site visit to the Czech Republic** — CPT inspectors visited detention and treatment facilities, interviewing detained persons, medical staff, administrators and officials.  
2. **Examination of forensic and psychiatric treatment practices** — The delegation reviewed how sex offenders were treated under protective treatment measures, including the use of surgical castration.  
3. **Collection of medical and legal information** — Inspectors examined documentation related to consent, medical approvals, court involvement and treatment outcomes.  
4. **Confidential report to Czech authorities** — After the visit, the CPT transmitted its findings and recommendations to the Czech government.  
5. **Government response** — Czech authorities submitted comments and explanations, including their position on the legality and regulation of the practice.  
6. **Publication** — The Council of Europe made the report public, together with the Czech government’s response, following the usual procedure in which publication occurs with the consent of the state concerned.

The publication brings renewed scrutiny to the Czech Republic’s handling of sex offenders in psychiatric and custodial settings and is likely to intensify debate over whether any form of irreversible bodily intervention can be justified in criminal justice treatment.

## Broader Human-Rights Implications

The report places the Czech Republic at the center of a wider European discussion about bodily integrity, medical ethics and the treatment of offenders with mental disorders.

The CPT’s mandate is not to determine criminal punishment policy, but to assess whether detained persons are protected from torture, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. In this case, the committee made clear that it views surgical castration as falling within the scope of those concerns.

The committee’s findings are likely to resonate beyond the Czech Republic, particularly in countries that continue to debate the use of medical interventions to manage sex-offender risk.

For the Council of Europe, the key issue is whether states can ever rely on the consent of detained and vulnerable offenders for a procedure that permanently alters the body and reproductive capacity. The CPT’s answer, as reflected in the newly published report, is unequivocal: surgical castration should be abandoned.
